title: Local vs. API Models
description: Hosted API models versus local models, quantized local inference in practice, privacy/cost/reliability tradeoffs, and a structured way to choose the right model for a given job.

lessons.title: Hosted API Models vs. Local Models
lessons.description: Compare the two fundamentally different ways to run an LLM in an application.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can name the core tradeoffs between calling a hosted API model and running a model locally.

sections.title: ☁️ Hosted API models: someone else runs the hardware
sections.content: A **hosted API model** runs on the provider's infrastructure; your application sends a request over the network and receives a response. You don't manage any hardware, and you typically get access to the largest, most capable models — but you pay per token, depend on network reliability, and send your data to a third party.

sections.title: 💻 Local models: you run the hardware
sections.content: A **local model** (typically an open-weight model, connecting back to the Hugging Face course's discussion of open weights vs. licenses) runs on your own hardware — a laptop, a server you control, or an on-premises deployment. You control data privacy fully and avoid per-token API costs, but you're responsible for hosting, and you're generally limited to smaller models than the largest hosted options, since your own hardware has to actually run it.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Assuming one approach is always better.** The right choice depends on your specific constraints (data sensitivity, budget, latency needs, required model capability) — there's no universal answer.

**Underestimating the operational burden of self-hosting.** Running your own inference infrastructure reliably at scale is genuine engineering work, not a one-time setup.

**Assuming a smaller local model is always 'worse' in a way that matters for the task.** For narrow, well-defined tasks, a smaller model can perform perfectly well — model size should match task difficulty, not default to 'biggest available'.

questions.question: What is the core difference between a hosted API model and a local model?
options: There is no real difference — both run in exactly the same way
A hosted API model runs on the provider's infrastructure and is accessed over the network, while a local model runs on hardware you control directly
Local models always cost more than hosted API models
Hosted API models cannot be used for any production application
questions.explanation: The fundamental distinction is where the model actually executes: a hosted API model runs remotely on the provider's servers, while a local model runs on infrastructure you manage yourself.

questions.question: What is a key advantage of running a local (open-weight) model instead of a hosted API model?
options: Local models are always more capable than any hosted API model
Full control over data privacy, since data never has to leave your own infrastructure, along with avoiding per-token API costs
Local models require no engineering effort to operate reliably
Local models automatically scale to any traffic volume with zero setup
questions.explanation: Since a local model runs entirely on infrastructure you control, sensitive data never needs to be sent to a third party, and there's no per-token API fee — though this comes with the tradeoff of managing your own hosting.

questions.question: Why is it a mistake to assume a smaller local model is always 'worse' in a way that matters?
options: Smaller models are always strictly worse for every possible task
For narrow, well-defined tasks, a smaller model can perform perfectly well, so the right model size should match the task's actual difficulty rather than defaulting to the largest available model
Model size has no relationship to task performance at all
Local models are never smaller than hosted API models
questions.explanation: Task difficulty, not raw model size, should drive the choice — a smaller model well-suited to a narrow, well-defined task can perform just as well as a larger one, while being cheaper and faster to run.

questions.question: What does this lesson identify as a downside of hosted API models compared to local models?
options: You pay per token, depend on network reliability, and send your data to a third party
Hosted API models require you to manage all the underlying hardware yourself
Hosted API models are always limited to smaller, less capable models
Hosted API models cannot be used for any production application
questions.explanation: The lesson lists per-token cost, network dependency, and sending data to a third party as the tradeoffs of using a hosted API model, in contrast to local deployment's control over data.

questions.question: How does this lesson connect local models back to the Hugging Face course?
options: It connects local models to that course's discussion of open weights vs. licenses
It claims the Hugging Face course never discussed local deployment at all
It says local models are unrelated to anything in the Hugging Face course
It states that only hosted models were covered by the Hugging Face course
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly ties the concept of a local model (typically open-weight) back to the open weights vs. licenses discussion from the Hugging Face course.

questions.question: Why does the lesson warn against underestimating the operational burden of self-hosting?
options: Because running your own inference infrastructure reliably at scale is genuine engineering work, not a one-time setup
Because self-hosting requires no ongoing maintenance whatsoever
Because hosted APIs actually require more operational effort than self-hosting
Because operational burden only applies to hosted API models, never local ones
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is underestimating that reliably running your own inference infrastructure at scale takes real, ongoing engineering effort rather than a single setup step.

questions.question: What does this lesson say you generally gain in exchange for the operational responsibility of running a local model?
options: Full control over data privacy and avoiding per-token API costs
Access to the largest and most capable models available anywhere
Guaranteed lower latency than any hosted API in every case
Automatic scaling to unlimited traffic with no configuration
questions.explanation: The lesson frames the tradeoff explicitly: running your own hardware brings full data privacy control and no per-token fees, at the cost of taking on hosting responsibility yourself.

questions.question: Why does the lesson say there's no universal answer to hosted vs. local deployment?
options: Because the right choice depends on specific constraints like data sensitivity, budget, latency needs, and required model capability
Because hosted deployment is always objectively the better choice in every situation
Because local deployment is always objectively the better choice in every situation
Because the choice has no real consequences either way
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly warns against assuming one approach is always better, since the right choice depends on the specific mix of constraints a given application actually faces.

lessons.title: Quantized Local Inference
lessons.description: See how quantization (from the Hugging Face course) makes running capable models locally practical.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain why quantization is often essential for running a capable model on consumer hardware.

sections.title: 🔢 The same idea, applied to inference this time
sections.content: The Hugging Face course covered quantization in the context of *training* (QLoRA). The same core idea — representing weights with fewer bits — applies to *inference* too: a model that would need far more memory than a typical laptop has at full precision can often run acceptably at 8-bit or 4-bit precision, fitting comfortably within consumer hardware limits.

sections.title: ⚙️ Local inference tooling
sections.content:
Tools built specifically for efficient local inference (like llama.cpp-style runtimes) are optimized to run quantized models efficiently on CPUs and consumer GPUs, exposing model choice, quantization level, and context length as configurable tradeoffs the developer picks explicitly.

```python
# Conceptual: same 7B-parameter model, different practical footprints
# 16-bit: ~14 GB   -> needs a capable GPU
# 8-bit:   ~7 GB   -> runs on many consumer GPUs
# 4-bit:  ~3.5 GB  -> can run on a laptop, sometimes CPU-only
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Assuming quantization is entirely free, with zero quality cost.** As covered in the Hugging Face course, there's typically a small quality tradeoff — worth validating for your specific task rather than assuming zero impact.

**Not checking hardware compatibility before committing to a quantization approach.** Not every quantization method is equally well supported across every hardware/software combination.

**Expecting a heavily quantized small local model to match a large hosted API model on every task.** Quantized local models are a genuine tool for the right job, not a universal drop-in replacement for the most capable hosted models.

questions.question: Why is quantization often essential for running a capable model on typical consumer hardware?
options: Quantization has no effect on how much hardware a model needs
A model that would require far more memory than consumer hardware has at full precision can often run acceptably at reduced precision (8-bit or 4-bit), fitting within realistic memory limits
Quantization only applies during training, never during inference
Consumer hardware can already run any model at full precision with no issue
questions.explanation: Just as quantization reduced memory needs for training in the Hugging Face course, applying it at inference time shrinks a model's memory footprint enough to fit on hardware that couldn't hold the full-precision version.

questions.question: What role do local inference tools like llama.cpp-style runtimes play?
options: They train new models from scratch on local hardware
They're optimized specifically to run quantized models efficiently on CPUs and consumer GPUs, exposing model choice and quantization level as configurable options
They only work with hosted API models, never local ones
They eliminate the need for quantization entirely
questions.explanation: These runtimes are purpose-built to make quantized local inference practical and efficient on ordinary consumer hardware, giving developers explicit control over tradeoffs like quantization level and context length.

questions.question: Why is it a mistake to expect a heavily quantized small local model to match a large hosted API model on every task?
options: Quantized local models always outperform large hosted API models on every task
Quantized local models are a genuine tool well-suited to certain jobs, but they aren't a universal drop-in replacement for the most capable hosted models on every kind of task
There is no meaningful capability difference between any two models regardless of size
Local models cannot be used for any real application
questions.explanation: Model capability still generally scales with size and training, so a small quantized local model is the right choice for tasks suited to its capability level — not an unconditional substitute for a much larger, more capable hosted model on every task.

questions.question: In the lesson's conceptual example, what happens to a 7B-parameter model's memory footprint at 4-bit precision compared to 16-bit?
options: It shrinks from roughly 14 GB down to about 3.5 GB
It stays exactly the same at both precisions
It increases significantly compared to 16-bit precision
4-bit precision is not mentioned in the example at all
questions.explanation: The lesson's example shows the same 7B model shrinking from ~14 GB at 16-bit to ~3.5 GB at 4-bit, illustrating how quantization reduces the practical hardware footprint.

questions.question: According to this lesson, in what earlier context did the Hugging Face course already cover the core idea behind quantization?
options: In the context of training, specifically QLoRA
In the context of tokenization only
In the context of dataset splitting
In the context of model licensing
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly recalls that the Hugging Face course covered quantization in the context of training (QLoRA), and this lesson applies the same core bit-reduction idea to inference instead.

questions.question: Why does the lesson caution against assuming quantization is entirely free with zero quality cost?
options: Because there's typically a small quality tradeoff, worth validating for your specific task
Because quantization always improves output quality with no downside
Because quantization has no effect on a model's output whatsoever
Because quality costs only occur with 16-bit precision, never with 4-bit
questions.explanation: The lesson notes that, as covered in the Hugging Face course, quantization typically carries a small quality tradeoff that's worth checking for your specific use case rather than assuming away.

questions.question: What should be checked before committing to a particular quantization approach, according to this lesson?
options: Hardware compatibility, since not every quantization method is equally well supported across every hardware/software combination
Nothing; all quantization methods work identically on any hardware
Only the model's original training dataset
Only whether the model was originally trained in 32-bit precision
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is not checking hardware compatibility first, since quantization method support can vary meaningfully across different hardware and software combinations.

questions.question: Why is it a mistake to expect a heavily quantized small local model to match a large hosted API model on every task, per this lesson?
options: Because quantized local models are a genuine tool for the right job, not a universal drop-in replacement for the most capable hosted models
Because quantized models are always strictly more capable than any hosted model
Because task difficulty has no bearing on which model size is appropriate
Because hosted API models never use any quantization themselves
questions.explanation: The lesson clarifies that quantized local models excel at certain jobs but shouldn't be expected to universally substitute for the largest, most capable hosted options on every kind of task.

lessons.title: Privacy, Cost, and Reliability Tradeoffs
lessons.description: Weigh the non-technical factors that often decide between hosted and local deployment.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can identify which deployment factors (privacy, cost structure, reliability) tend to favor hosted vs. local models.

sections.title: 🔒 Privacy and compliance
sections.content: For data with strict regulatory or contractual privacy requirements (healthcare, legal, certain financial data), sending it to a third-party hosted API may not be permissible at all — a strong argument for local deployment, regardless of the capability tradeoff, in exactly the kinds of regulated contexts where this matters most.

sections.title: 💵 Cost structure: per-request vs. fixed infrastructure
sections.content: Hosted APIs charge per token used — costs scale directly (and sometimes unpredictably) with usage. Local deployment has a more fixed cost structure (hardware, hosting, and maintenance) that doesn't scale per-request in the same way — at high enough sustained volume, the economics can favor local; at low or spiky volume, they usually favor hosted.

sections.title: 🌐 Reliability and dependency
sections.content: A hosted API introduces a dependency on the provider's uptime, rate limits, and pricing changes — outside your direct control. Local deployment brings that reliability fully in-house, at the cost of you being responsible for maintaining it.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Deciding purely on technical capability while ignoring privacy/compliance requirements.** For regulated data, the compliance answer can override an otherwise reasonable technical preference.

**Ignoring usage volume when comparing cost structures.** The 'cheaper' option genuinely depends on your actual traffic pattern, not a one-size-fits-all rule.

**Treating a hosted API provider's uptime and pricing as guaranteed forever.** Building in a fallback plan (an alternative provider, a local fallback model) protects against a single point of dependency.

questions.question: Why might data with strict regulatory or contractual privacy requirements favor local deployment over a hosted API?
options: Privacy requirements never have any bearing on the choice of deployment

Sending certain sensitive data to a third-party hosted API may not be permissible under regulatory or contractual privacy requirements, making local deployment a compliance necessity rather than just a preference
Hosted APIs are always more secure than local deployment regardless of context
Local deployment automatically violates privacy requirements
questions.explanation: For data governed by strict regulatory or contractual privacy rules, a third-party hosted API may simply be off the table, making local deployment the compliant choice regardless of any other technical tradeoff.

questions.question: How does the cost structure of hosted APIs differ from local deployment?
options: Both have identical cost structures with no meaningful difference
Hosted APIs charge per token used, scaling directly with usage, while local deployment has more fixed infrastructure costs that don't scale per-request the same way
Local deployment always charges per token, just like hosted APIs
Hosted APIs have no cost at all
questions.explanation: Hosted API cost scales with actual usage (per token), while local deployment's cost is dominated by more fixed hardware and maintenance expenses — meaning the economically favorable option genuinely depends on your traffic volume.

questions.question: Why is it risky to treat a hosted API provider's uptime and pricing as permanently guaranteed?
options: Hosted API providers never change their pricing or experience any downtime
A hosted API introduces a dependency outside your direct control, so building a fallback plan protects against a single point of failure if uptime, rate limits, or pricing change
This risk only applies to local deployments, never to hosted APIs
There is no way to mitigate dependency risk on a hosted provider
questions.explanation: Relying on any single external provider creates a dependency you don't fully control — planning a fallback (an alternate provider or local option) is a reasonable hedge against changes in that provider's uptime, limits, or pricing.

questions.question: What specific domains does this lesson name as examples where sending data to a hosted API may not be permissible?
options: Healthcare, legal, and certain financial data
Weather forecasting, sports statistics, and public news data
Publicly available open-source code repositories
Any data that has already been published on the internet
questions.explanation: The lesson specifically names healthcare, legal, and certain financial data as examples of contexts with strict privacy or regulatory requirements that can rule out sending data to a hosted API.

questions.question: According to this lesson, at what usage pattern does local deployment's cost structure tend to become more favorable?
options: At high enough sustained volume
At very low, infrequent, or spiky usage
Local deployment is never more cost-favorable regardless of volume
Cost favorability has nothing to do with usage volume
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that local deployment's more fixed cost structure tends to favor it at high sustained volume, while hosted APIs usually favor low or spiky usage patterns.

questions.question: What specific dependency risk does relying on a hosted API introduce, according to this lesson?
options: A dependency on the provider's uptime, rate limits, and pricing changes, all outside your direct control
No dependency risk at all, since hosted APIs are always fully reliable
A dependency that only affects local deployments, not hosted ones
A dependency solely on your own internal network infrastructure
questions.explanation: The lesson identifies uptime, rate limits, and pricing changes as dependency risks that come with relying on an external hosted API provider outside your own control.

questions.question: Why does the lesson warn against deciding purely on technical capability while ignoring privacy/compliance requirements?
options: Because for regulated data, the compliance answer can override an otherwise reasonable technical preference
Because compliance requirements never actually affect deployment decisions in practice
Because technical capability is always the only factor that matters
Because privacy and compliance are identical concepts with no practical difference
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is ignoring compliance requirements in favor of pure technical preference — for regulated data, compliance can override what would otherwise be the preferred technical choice.

questions.question: Why does this lesson recommend building in a fallback plan against a hosted provider's uptime or pricing changes?
options: Because treating a provider's uptime and pricing as guaranteed forever is risky; a fallback protects against a single point of dependency
Because hosted providers never change their pricing or experience downtime
Because fallback plans are unnecessary once a provider is selected
Because this risk applies only to local deployments, never hosted ones
questions.explanation: The lesson warns against assuming a provider's terms are permanent, recommending a fallback (an alternative provider or local option) as protection against that single point of dependency.

lessons.title: Choosing the Right Model for the Job
lessons.description: Bring the deployment and capability tradeoffs together into an actual decision framework.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can walk through a structured set of questions for choosing a model and deployment approach for a given task.

sections.title: ❓ Questions worth asking before picking a model
sections.content: Before defaulting to 'the biggest, most capable model available', it's worth explicitly asking: How sensitive is the data (privacy/compliance)? What's the actual required capability level for this specific task, not a hypothetical hardest case? What's the expected traffic volume and latency requirement? What's the budget, and how does it compare across hosted vs. local at your expected volume?

sections.title: 🎯 Matching model to task, not defaulting to 'biggest'
sections.content:
A simple classification or extraction task might be handled perfectly well by a small, fast, cheap model (hosted or local); a task requiring deep, multi-step reasoning over ambiguous instructions might genuinely need the largest available hosted model. The engineering skill here is matching capability to actual requirement, not reflexively reaching for the most powerful (and most expensive) option every time.

```python
# Conceptual decision sketch:
# sensitive data + moderate task difficulty -> local, quantized model
# low sensitivity + high task difficulty -> large hosted API model
# low sensitivity + simple task + high volume -> small hosted or local model, optimized for cost
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Choosing a model once and never revisiting the decision.** Requirements change (traffic grows, new privacy rules apply, better/cheaper models become available) — this decision deserves periodic reassessment, not permanence.

**Optimizing model choice for the hardest hypothetical case instead of the actual typical case.** This is a common source of overpaying for capability the task doesn't usually need.

**Ignoring that model routing (from the earlier cost/latency lesson) can combine multiple models rather than forcing a single choice.** Many production systems use several models together, each matched to a different part of the workload.

questions.question: What questions should be asked before defaulting to the largest, most capable available model?
options: None — the largest model should always be used regardless of context
How sensitive is the data, what capability level the task actually requires, expected traffic volume and latency needs, and budget across hosted vs. local options
Only the total number of parameters the model has
Only whether the model is open-weight or not
questions.explanation: A deliberate model choice weighs data sensitivity, actual required capability, traffic and latency needs, and budget — rather than skipping straight to whichever model is most capable on paper.

questions.question: Why is matching model capability to actual task requirement better than always choosing the most powerful available model?
options: The most powerful model is always the cheapest and fastest option too
Using a more powerful (and typically more expensive, slower) model than a task actually requires means overpaying for capability the task doesn't need
Task difficulty has no relationship to which model should be chosen
Smaller models can never handle any real production task
questions.explanation: Since capability, cost, and latency are linked, defaulting to the most powerful model regardless of task difficulty means paying for (and waiting on) capability that a simpler, cheaper, faster model could have provided just as well.

questions.question: Why should model choice be revisited periodically rather than decided once and left permanent?
options: Model choice should never be reconsidered once initially made
Requirements change over time — traffic grows, new privacy rules may apply, and better or cheaper models become available — so periodic reassessment keeps the choice aligned with current conditions
Models never improve or change over time, so reassessment is pointless
Traffic volume and privacy requirements never actually change for a real application
questions.explanation: Since the factors driving model choice (traffic, privacy rules, available model options) evolve over time, treating the decision as permanent risks running on an outdated choice — periodic reassessment keeps it matched to current, not historical, conditions.

questions.question: In the lesson's conceptual decision sketch, what deployment choice is suggested for sensitive data combined with moderate task difficulty?
options: A local, quantized model
The largest available hosted API model
No model at all; the task should be done manually
A model chosen at random regardless of sensitivity
questions.explanation: The lesson's decision sketch specifically pairs sensitive data and moderate task difficulty with a local, quantized model as the recommended approach.

questions.question: According to this lesson, what should drive the required capability question when choosing a model?
options: The actual required capability level for the specific task, not a hypothetical hardest case
Only the model's total number of parameters, regardless of the task
The single hardest possible case the task could theoretically involve
Whichever model happens to be newest on the market
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly frames the capability question around the task's actual requirement, warning separately against optimizing for a hypothetical hardest case rather than the real typical one.

questions.question: Why does this lesson connect model choice to model routing from the earlier cost/latency lesson?
options: Because many production systems combine multiple models together, each matched to a different part of the workload, rather than forcing a single choice
Because model routing makes it impossible to ever choose more than one model
Because routing and model choice are entirely unrelated concepts
Because routing eliminates the need to ever consider model capability
questions.explanation: The lesson notes that ignoring model routing is a common mistake, since it lets a system combine several models — each suited to a different part of the workload — instead of settling on one single model for everything.

questions.question: Why does the lesson warn against optimizing model choice for the hardest hypothetical case instead of the actual typical case?
options: Because this is a common source of overpaying for capability the task doesn't usually need
Because the hardest hypothetical case is always identical to the typical case
Because optimizing for the hardest case always reduces cost and latency
Because typical cases never actually occur in real production systems
questions.explanation: The lesson identifies this as a common mistake: defaulting to worst-case capability planning usually means paying for more capability than the task actually needs most of the time.

questions.question: Why should the model and deployment choice be periodically reassessed, according to this lesson?
options: Because requirements change over time — traffic grows, new privacy rules may apply, and better or cheaper models become available
Because model choice, once made, technically cannot be changed afterward
Because reassessment has no practical benefit once a model is chosen
Because privacy rules and traffic patterns never actually change after launch
questions.explanation: The lesson recommends revisiting the decision periodically since the underlying factors — traffic, privacy rules, available models — evolve, and a one-time decision can become outdated.
